title: How No-fly Zones Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain no-fly zones, starting with the early history of military aircraft (Wright brothers, the War Department, the 1937 bombing of Guernica) and then covering the three no-fly zones used so far: Iraq (1991, Operation Provide Comfort and the southern zone, protecting Kurds and Shiites after the Gulf War), Bosnia (early 1990s, Operation Deny Flight, NATO, against Bosnian Serb aircraft), and Libya (2011, Operation Odyssey Dawn, under UN Security Council Resolution 1973). They discuss the UN Charter Chapter VII process, the permanent Security Council members' vetoes and abstentions, rules of engagement, the shootdown of Scott O'Grady over Bosnia, and whether no-fly zones are effective. The episode opens with banter about the TV show The Newsroom and West Wing and closes with a listener mail shout-out to a civics teacher, Mr. Kristof, and a mention of Iraqi dinar investing.

segments.title: Opening banter on TV shows
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about the film Network and Aaron Sorkin shows, including The Newsroom and The West Wing, and Paul Schneider.

segments.title: Early military aircraft history
segments.summary: Josh recounts how the Wright brothers offered their plane to the War Department, which turned them down, until the Post Office used planes to carry mail. Planes were soon militarized, and the 1937 bombing of Guernica by Spanish fascist forces is described as an early use against civilians.

segments.title: What a no-fly zone is and why it is significant
segments.summary: The hosts explain that a no-fly zone intervenes in a sovereign nation's airspace to protect civilians, and that it requires a United Nations mandate. They note only three have been used, and that the first was in the early 1990s.

segments.title: Iraq no-fly zone after the Gulf War
segments.summary: After Saddam Hussein's forces crushed Kurdish and Shiite uprisings encouraged by US broadcasts, the UN authorized humanitarian aid and no-fly zones north of the 36th parallel and south of the 32nd parallel. Enforcement involved shooting down aircraft and striking ground radar and military targets, and the zones lasted until 2003.

segments.title: Bosnia no-fly zone (Operation Deny Flight)
segments.summary: NATO established a no-fly zone over Bosnia and Herzegovina, named Operation Deny Flight, to block Bosnian Serb military aircraft attacking Muslim neighbors. It was more aggressive, including striking military installations.

segments.title: Libya no-fly zone (Operation Odyssey Dawn) and UN process
segments.summary: In 2011, UN Security Council Resolution 1973 authorized a no-fly zone over Libya, and a US and UK-led NATO coalition struck Libyan air defenses on the first day, including Tomahawk missiles. The hosts describe the Security Council vote, where China and Russia abstained, and the Chapter VII process and rules of engagement.

segments.title: Shootdowns, Scott O'Grady, and effectiveness
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the risk of pilots being shot down, recounting Scott O'Grady's shootdown over Bosnia and six days of evasion. They debate whether the Libya intervention was effective and note that the Srebrenica massacre happened despite the Bosnia zone.

segments.title: Iraqi dinar scam aside and closing topics
segments.summary: A brief sidebar warns listeners against investing in Iraqi dinar, and the hosts reminisce about Three Kings and Uncommon Valor before wrapping up the no-fly zone discussion.

segments.title: Listener mail: civics teacher shout-out
segments.summary: A listener named Jack asks for a shout-out to his civics teacher Mr. Kristof and math teacher Mrs. Kristof, who use the show in class.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and point listeners to HowStuffWorks for more on no-fly zones.
